1 Nephi 1:1.context: These are the very first words of the Book of Mormon, written by Nephi, the son of Lehi and Sariah. Nephi wrote them many years after his family left Jerusalem around 600 BC, looking back on his life as a grown man and a prophet. He is writing to anyone who will someday read his record, including us. He begins by thanking his "goodly parents" for teaching him, and he admits that he faced many hard trials in his life. Even so, he says he was greatly blessed by the Lord and came to know God's goodness. His main point is that a person can have real troubles and still be deeply blessed, and that knowing God's goodness is why he wanted to keep a record.

1 Nephi 3:7.context: Lehi's family had left Jerusalem and was camped in the wilderness when the Lord told Lehi in a dream to send his sons back for the brass plates. Those plates held the scriptures and the history of their ancestors, but they were kept by a powerful man named Laban, so the task seemed hard and even dangerous. Laman and Lemuel complained, but Nephi spoke these words to his father, Lehi. Nephi promised to "go and do" what the Lord had commanded, because he trusted that God never gives a commandment without preparing a way to keep it. His main point is that we can obey the Lord with faith, even when we do not yet know how things will work out, because God will help us.

1 Nephi 8:10.context: In this chapter Lehi tells his family about a dream, or vision, he had while they were living in the wilderness, and Nephi writes it down. Lehi is speaking to his children, and he is especially worried about his sons Laman and Lemuel. After traveling through a dark and dreary place, Lehi sees a tree whose fruit could make a person happy. When he tasted it, the fruit was sweeter and whiter than anything he had ever known, and it filled him with joy. Later in the Book of Mormon we learn that this tree stands for the love of God, shown most of all through the gift of Jesus Christ. The main point is that God's love is the greatest source of happiness, and He invites everyone to come and receive it.

1 Nephi 11:17.context: After hearing about his father Lehi's dream, Nephi wanted to see and understand it for himself, and as he sat pondering, the Lord answered with a vision. In this verse Nephi is speaking with an angel who is guiding him through what he sees. Nephi has just seen a beautiful young woman in the city of Nazareth, and the angel asks him if he understands the "condescension of God," which means God coming down from His heavenly place to help His children. Nephi answers honestly that he knows God loves His children, even though he does not understand everything. The angel then tells him that the young woman, Mary, would be the mother of the Son of God. The main point is that we can trust in God's love even when we do not have all the answers.

1 Nephi 11:25.context: Nephi is describing his own vision, in which an angel helped him understand the meaning of his father Lehi's dream. In the vision Nephi has just seen the baby Jesus and then the Savior's ministry among the people. Writing for his future readers, Nephi explains two key symbols from the dream. The rod of iron is the word of God, which leads people safely to the tree of life, and both the fountain of living waters and the tree represent the love of God. The main point is that holding tightly to God's word will lead us to Jesus Christ and to the joy of feeling God's love.

1 Nephi 17:3.context: Nephi is writing about the eight long years his family spent traveling through the wilderness after leaving Jerusalem. During that time they faced great hardships, children were born along the way, and the Lord made it so they could eat their meat raw without cooking fires. Looking back, Nephi stops to teach his readers a lesson from all of this. He says that when people keep God's commandments, the Lord nourishes them, strengthens them, and gives them the means to do what He asks. His main point is that God does not leave His faithful children alone in hard times, even though He does not always make the path easy.

1 Nephi 19:23.context: By this point Lehi's family has crossed the ocean and settled in the promised land, and Nephi is teaching his brothers and their families. Nephi explains that he read them many things from the books of Moses on the brass plates. To help them believe more fully in the Lord their Redeemer, he also read them the words of the prophet Isaiah. He says he would "liken all scriptures" to his people, meaning he showed how the scriptures applied to their own lives. His main point is that scriptures written long ago can teach and help us today when we look for how they fit our own lives.

1 Nephi 21:16.context: In this chapter Nephi is reading the words of the prophet Isaiah from the brass plates to his brothers, so these are Isaiah's words, quoted by Nephi. In the passage, the Lord is speaking to the house of Israel, which has felt forgotten and forsaken. Just before this verse, the Lord asks whether a mother could forget her own baby, and He says that even if she could, He will never forget His people. Then He says He has "graven," or engraved, them on the palms of His hands, which reminds us of the marks of the nails in the Savior's hands. The main point is that Jesus Christ always remembers the people He has redeemed, and His love is even stronger than a loving parent's.

2 Nephi 1:15.context: This verse comes from 2 Nephi 1, where Lehi, now old and near the end of his life in the promised land, gathers his family to give them his last counsel. He is speaking especially to his older sons, Laman and Lemuel, whom he has just begged to wake up from spiritual sleep and shake off the chains of sin. Lehi tells them that he will soon be laid in the grave, but he is not afraid. He testifies that the Lord has rescued his soul from hell, that he has seen the Lord's glory, and that he feels surrounded forever by God's love. Lehi wants his sons to see that this same peace and redemption can be theirs if they will remember and keep the Lord's commandments.

2 Nephi 2:8.context: In 2 Nephi 2, Lehi gives a final blessing and teaching to his son Jacob, who was born in the wilderness and had known affliction and sorrow as a child. Lehi explains that the law by itself cannot save anyone, because everyone falls short of it. In this verse he says that no one can live in God's presence except through the merits, mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah, Jesus Christ. He adds that Christ would lay down His life and take it up again, becoming the first to rise from the dead so that all could be resurrected. Lehi says it is very important to make these things known to everyone on the earth. His main point is that we are saved by relying on Jesus Christ, whose Atonement can truly change and heal us when we repent.

2 Nephi 2:11.context: Lehi is still speaking to his son Jacob, whom he calls his firstborn in the wilderness, as part of his final teachings before he dies. He has been explaining God's plan, and here he teaches that there must be opposition in all things. Without opposites like good and bad, holiness and misery, or happiness and sadness, nothing would have meaning, and life would be like a body that is not alive at all. Opposition gives us real choices, and our choices bring consequences that help us learn and grow. Jacob had suffered much as a child, so this teaching helped him see that even hard things can have a purpose in Heavenly Father's plan.

2 Nephi 2:25.context: This verse is part of Lehi's last teachings to his son Jacob in 2 Nephi 2, where he explains the Creation, the Fall of Adam and Eve, and the Atonement of Jesus Christ. Lehi teaches that if Adam and Eve had not eaten the forbidden fruit, they would have stayed in the Garden of Eden in a state of innocence and could not have had children. Because they fell, they became mortal, had a family, and began the whole human family on the earth. Lehi explains that all of this happened according to the wisdom of God, who knows all things. In this short verse he sums it up: Adam fell so that people could exist, and people exist so that they can have joy. His point is that the Fall was a needed part of Heavenly Father's plan, and that God's purpose for His children is their happiness.

2 Nephi 2:27.context: Near the end of 2 Nephi 2, Lehi is finishing his final teachings to Jacob and his other sons before his death. He has just explained that the Messiah would come to redeem everyone from the Fall, making them free to act for themselves. In this verse Lehi teaches that every person is free to choose. They can choose liberty and eternal life through Jesus Christ, the great Mediator, or they can choose captivity and death by following the devil, who wants everyone to be miserable like himself. Lehi wants his family to understand that God gives us agency and wants us to have joy, and he urges them to choose Christ and eternal life.

2 Nephi 4:15.context: In 2 Nephi 4, Nephi is writing after the death of his father, Lehi, at a time when Laman, Lemuel, and the sons of Ishmael had become angry with him. He explains that on these plates he writes the things of his soul, along with many scriptures from the brass plates. Nephi says his soul delights in the scriptures, that his heart ponders them, and that he writes them down so his children can learn from them. This verse begins a heartfelt passage often called the psalm of Nephi, where he pours out his deepest feelings to the Lord. His example teaches that we can delight in the scriptures, think deeply about them, and live by them so our families can follow.

2 Nephi 4:34.context: This verse comes at the end of what is often called the psalm of Nephi in 2 Nephi 4, written after his father Lehi died and his older brothers grew angry with him. In this poem Nephi is honest about feeling discouraged and sorrowful because of his weaknesses and sins. Then he remembers all the Lord has done for him, from leading him through the wilderness to protecting him on the ocean, and he cries out to the Lord in prayer. In this verse Nephi declares that he has trusted the Lord and will trust Him forever. He says he will not put his trust in the arm of flesh, meaning human strength or the wisdom of people. His main point is that lasting peace and strength come from relying on God rather than on ourselves or others.

2 Nephi 9:28.context: 2 Nephi 9 is part of a sermon by Jacob, Nephi's younger brother, which Nephi included in his record. Jacob had been called as a teacher among the Nephites, and he was speaking to his people about the Atonement of Jesus Christ and God's great plan. Here he contrasts God's merciful plan with the cunning plan of the evil one, and he warns about a trap that catches many people. When people become learned, they sometimes think they are wise and set aside God's counsel, believing they know better on their own. Jacob teaches that this kind of wisdom is really foolishness, but in the very next verse he adds that being learned is good if we listen to the counsels of God. His point is that education is valuable, but true knowledge also comes from God and the Holy Ghost, so learning should never replace humility.

2 Nephi 9:39.context: This verse is from Jacob's sermon in 2 Nephi 9, which Nephi recorded in his writings. Jacob, Nephi's younger brother and a teacher among the Nephites, was speaking to his people, whom he lovingly calls his beloved brethren. Just before this verse, he gives a list of warnings, or woes, against sins such as lying, worshipping idols, and dying without repenting. Here he pleads with them to remember how serious it is to sin against a holy God and to give in to the temptations of Satan, the cunning one. He teaches that being carnally minded, or focused only on worldly and selfish desires, leads to spiritual death, while being spiritually minded leads to eternal life. Jacob wants his people to set their hearts and thoughts on God so they can come unto the Holy One of Israel.

2 Nephi 9:51.context: Near the end of his sermon in 2 Nephi 9, Jacob, Nephi's younger brother and a teacher among the Nephites, speaks tenderly to his people. In the verse just before this one, he echoes words from Isaiah, inviting everyone who thirsts to come and receive without money, showing that the Lord's salvation is offered freely to all. Then he counsels them not to spend their money on things that have no real worth, or their labor on things that can never satisfy. Instead, he invites them to come unto the Holy One of Israel and feast on what never spoils or wears out. Jacob's point is that worldly things leave us empty, but coming to Jesus Christ fills the soul with lasting joy.

2 Nephi 25:23.context: In 2 Nephi 25, Nephi is writing near the end of his record, after quoting many chapters of Isaiah, and he now speaks plainly about Jesus Christ. Here he is addressing his own children and the descendants of Lehi who would read his words in the future. He explains that he and his people work hard to write their record so that their children and their brethren will believe in Christ and be reconciled to God. He adds that we are saved by grace, after all we can do. Grace is the help and power that comes through Jesus Christ's mercy, and our own efforts, like repenting and keeping the commandments, show our faith in Him. Nephi's main point is that salvation comes through Christ, and he deeply wanted his family to put their trust in the Savior.

2 Nephi 25:26.context: This verse is part of Nephi's plain teaching about Jesus Christ in 2 Nephi 25, written after he had shared many of Isaiah's prophecies. Nephi is writing especially for his own children and descendants, and he explains why his people still kept the law of Moses even though they believed in Christ. He says that they talk of Christ, rejoice in Christ, preach of Christ, prophesy of Christ, and write about Christ. They do all this so their children will know where to look for forgiveness of their sins. Nephi's main point is that Jesus Christ is the source of forgiveness and joy, and his example invites us to speak openly about the Savior with our own families.

2 Nephi 26:33.context: In 2 Nephi 26, Nephi is prophesying about the future and writing to the Gentiles and all who would one day read his words, teaching how the Lord treats all His children. Just before this verse, he lists sins the Lord has forbidden, such as priestcraft, lying, stealing, envy, and contention. Here he explains that none of these evils come from the Lord, who does only good and makes His ways plain. Nephi teaches that the Lord invites everyone to come unto Him and share in His goodness, and that He turns no one away, whatever their race, whether they are free or enslaved, male or female. Nephi's main point is that God loves all His children, His Atonement is for everyone, and all are alike unto Him.

2 Nephi 28:30.context: In 2 Nephi 28, Nephi prophesies about the last days, when the Book of Mormon would come forth, and he warns about false ideas Satan would spread. He is writing for people in our day, and he describes those who would say they have received the word of God and need no more because they have enough. In this verse Nephi shares the Lord's answer: God gives truth to His children line upon line and precept upon precept, a little at a time. Those who listen to His counsel will learn wisdom and receive more, but those who say they have enough will lose even what they have. Nephi's point is that God still speaks today, and we should keep our hearts open to receive more of His word.

2 Nephi 31:20.context: In 2 Nephi 31, Nephi is near the end of his record and writes his final teachings, which he calls the doctrine of Christ. He is writing to his beloved brethren, meaning his people and all who will read his words, after explaining how Jesus Christ was baptized to show us the way. Nephi teaches that after we enter the strait and narrow path through repentance, baptism, and receiving the Holy Ghost, our work is not finished. In this verse he says we must press forward with steadfastness in Christ, with a bright hope and love for God and all people, feasting on the words of Christ and enduring to the end. He promises that those who do this will receive eternal life. His main point is that following Christ is a lifelong journey of faithfully keeping our covenants day after day.

2 Nephi 31:21.context: This verse closes 2 Nephi 31, where Nephi, near the end of his record, explains the doctrine of Christ to his beloved brethren and to all future readers. He has just taught that we enter the path to eternal life through faith in Jesus Christ, repentance, baptism, and the gift of the Holy Ghost, and that we must then press forward and endure to the end. In this verse he declares that this is the way, and there is no other way or name under heaven by which anyone can be saved in the kingdom of God. He calls it the doctrine of Christ, the one true doctrine of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, who are one God. Nephi's main point is that Jesus Christ and His gospel are the only path back to Heavenly Father, and that path, though sometimes hard, leads to great joy.

2 Nephi 32:3.context: In 2 Nephi 32, Nephi continues his final teachings to his beloved brethren, his people and all who would read his record. He senses that they are wondering what they should do after they have entered the path by being baptized and receiving the Holy Ghost. He reminds them that he had said they could speak with the tongue of angels, and he explains that angels speak by the power of the Holy Ghost, so they speak the words of Christ. Then he invites them to feast upon the words of Christ, because those words will tell them everything they should do. Feasting means more than a quick taste; it means studying, pondering, and living Christ's words until they become part of us. Nephi's main point is that the words of Christ, together with the Holy Ghost, can guide us in every part of our lives.

2 Nephi 32:9.context: Near the very end of his writings in 2 Nephi 32, Nephi is giving final counsel to his beloved brethren and to all who would read his words. He is saddened that some are still unsure what to do, and he explains that the Spirit teaches people to pray, while the evil spirit teaches them not to pray. In this verse Nephi says we must pray always and not give up. He teaches that before we do anything for the Lord, we should first pray to the Father in the name of Christ, asking Him to consecrate, or bless, what we do. Then our efforts will be for the good of our souls. Nephi's main point is that prayer keeps us connected to God and invites His help in everything we do.

Jacob 2:18.context: Jacob, Nephi's younger brother, was a prophet and teacher among the Nephites after Nephi died. In this chapter he is speaking at the temple to the Nephite people, because the Lord had given him an errand to warn them about their sins. Many Nephites had found gold and silver and had become proud, thinking they were better than others and refusing to share with those in need. Jacob tells them that before they seek riches, they should seek the kingdom of God. In the next verse he explains that those who have a hope in Christ will use any riches to do good, such as feeding the hungry and helping the sick. His main point is that God should come first in our lives, and that the things we are blessed with should be used to bless others.

Enos 1:4.context: Enos was the son of the prophet Jacob, and here he writes about a day that changed his life. He had gone into the forest to hunt animals, and the words he had often heard his father speak about eternal life and joy sank deep into his heart. Writing to his future readers, Enos says his soul "hungered," meaning he deeply longed to be close to God. He knelt down and prayed with all his heart all day long, and when night came he was still praying. Soon afterward the Lord told him that his sins were forgiven because of his faith in Christ. The main point is that God hears sincere prayers, and when we truly seek Him, He answers.

Jarom 1:5.context: Jarom was the son of Enos and the grandson of Jacob, and he received the small plates from his father to keep the family's sacred record. He wrote only a short book, and in it he describes how the Nephites were doing about two hundred years after Lehi's family left Jerusalem. Writing to future readers, Jarom reports that the people had grown strong and were keeping the law of Moses and the Sabbath day holy. He adds that they did not speak against God or use His name in vain, and that their laws were very strict. A few verses later he explains that because the people stayed faithful, the Lord blessed and protected them. The main point is that a people who honor God and keep His commandments are blessed and strengthened by Him.

Omni 1:26.context: Amaleki was the last person to write in the small plates of Nephi, and he was getting old and had no children to pass the record to. He decided to give the plates to the righteous King Benjamin, and before he finished, he left a final message for his readers, whom he calls his "beloved brethren." Amaleki invites everyone to come unto Christ, the Holy One of Israel, and receive His salvation and redeeming power. He tells them to offer their "whole souls" to Christ, to keep fasting and praying, and to endure to the end. He promises that those who do this will be saved. His main point is that coming to Christ means giving Him our whole hearts, not just part of them.

Words of Mormon 1:7.context: Mormon, the prophet who put together most of the Book of Mormon, wrote this short book hundreds of years after Christ came, near the end of the Nephite nation. While making a shortened history from the large plates, he found the small plates of Nephi, full of prophecies about Christ, and he felt he should include them with his record. Writing to his future readers, Mormon says he is doing this "for a wise purpose," because the Spirit of the Lord was whispering to him. He admits he does not know all things, but the Lord knows everything that will happen. Centuries later, when 116 pages of Joseph Smith's first translation were lost, the small plates helped provide that early part of the story. The main point is that following the Spirit, even when we do not understand why, lets the Lord work His purposes through us.

Mosiah 2:17.context: King Benjamin is speaking near the end of his life, after his people gathered at the temple to hear him and to see his son Mosiah named as the next king. He is talking to his whole nation, so many people that he had a tower built so more of them could hear. Benjamin has just reminded them that as king he worked with his own hands and spent his life serving them instead of making them serve him. In this verse he explains why he did it: when we serve the people around us, we are really serving God. His main point is that helping others is one of the truest ways to show our love for Heavenly Father. He wants his people, and us, to look for chances to serve someone every day.

Mosiah 2:41.context: King Benjamin is still speaking to his people gathered around the temple, at the close of the first part of his great sermon. Just before this, he warned them about the sad state of people who know God's commandments and choose to rebel against them. Now he turns to the bright side and asks them to think about the "blessed and happy state" of those who keep the commandments. He promises that obedient people are blessed in both everyday and spiritual things, and if they stay faithful to the end they will live with God in never-ending happiness. His main point is that keeping God's commandments is the path to real, lasting joy. He ends by pleading with them to remember that these things are true because the Lord Himself has said them.

Mosiah 3:19.context: These words come from an angel who visited King Benjamin, and Benjamin is repeating the angel's message to his people gathered at the temple. The angel taught about Jesus Christ, who would come to earth, suffer for our sins, and make it possible for us to be saved. In this verse the angel explains that because of the Fall of Adam, our fallen "natural" side pulls us away from God. But we can put off that natural self by following the promptings of the Holy Ghost and becoming a saint through the Atonement of Christ. The angel describes what that changed person is like: humble, meek, patient, full of love, and willing to accept even the hard things the Lord allows in their life, the way a child trusts a loving father. The main point is that through Jesus Christ our very nature can change so that we become more like Him.

Mosiah 4:9.context: King Benjamin is speaking to his people at the temple right after they had fallen to the ground, cried out for mercy through Jesus Christ, and felt the joy of having their sins forgiven. He now teaches them what they need to keep believing and doing. In this verse he invites them to believe that God is real, that He created everything in heaven and on earth, and that He has all wisdom and all power. He also reminds them that people cannot understand everything the Lord understands. His main point is that we can fully trust God because He knows and can do far more than we can. This trust is the foundation for the repentance and humility he teaches in the next verses.

Mosiah 4:27.context: King Benjamin is still teaching his people at the temple, and he has just told them to care for the poor, feed the hungry, and help those in need. Because that is a big job, he adds some wise counsel in this verse. He tells them to do all these good things "in wisdom and order," because no one is expected to run faster than they have strength. At the same time, he says they should still work hard and be diligent so they can win the prize. His main point is that the Lord wants us to do our best without wearing ourselves out, focusing our limited time and energy on what matters most. When we try to do more than we are able, we just get tired, but steady, wise effort helps us keep serving.

Mosiah 4:30.context: King Benjamin is finishing this part of his sermon to his people gathered at the temple. He explains that he cannot list every possible way a person could sin, because there are too many. Instead, he gives them a simple guide: watch your thoughts, your words, and your actions. He tells them to keep God's commandments and keep their faith in the coming of Jesus Christ for the rest of their lives. His main point is that each of us is responsible for paying attention to how we think, speak, and act, and how those choices affect ourselves, others, and our relationship with God. He closes with a loving warning to remember these things and not perish.

Mosiah 5:2.context: In this verse the speakers are King Benjamin's people, answering him all together with one voice after hearing his sermon at the temple. Benjamin had sent out to ask whether they believed what he taught them. They reply that they believe every word and know it is true because the Spirit of the Lord has worked a "mighty change" in their hearts. Because of that change, they say, they no longer want to do evil but want to do good all the time. The main point is that the Holy Ghost can change not just what we do but what we desire, and that is what true conversion looks like. This change can happen gradually or all at once, and it helps us resist temptation.

Mosiah 5:13.context: King Benjamin is speaking to his people at the temple after they have made a covenant to obey God and have taken upon themselves the name of Jesus Christ. He has just urged them to remember that name always so it stays written in their hearts. In this verse he asks a thoughtful question: how can someone know a master they have never served, who is a stranger to them and far from their thoughts? He is teaching that we come to know Jesus Christ by serving Him and keeping Him in our thoughts and in the desires of our hearts. His main point is that if we want Christ to know us and call us His, we must stay close to Him through daily service and remembrance. Benjamin wants his people to treat their covenant as a real, ongoing relationship with the Savior.

Mosiah 18:8.context: Alma is speaking at the Waters of Mormon, a place with a fountain of pure water where he secretly taught people the gospel. Alma had once been a priest of wicked King Noah, but he believed Abinadi's testimony, repented, and had to hide from the king. Here he is talking to a group of people who believed his teachings and wanted to be baptized. He explains that if they want to join God's fold and be called His people, they must be willing to bear one another's burdens so those burdens feel lighter. His main point is that the covenant of baptism is a promise to God that also changes how we treat each other. When we join the Lord's people, we promise to help carry each other's loads.

Mosiah 18:9.context: Alma is continuing to teach the believers gathered at the Waters of Mormon, who want to be baptized. In this verse he lists more of the promises that come with the baptismal covenant. They must be willing to mourn with those who are sad, comfort those who need comfort, and stand as witnesses of God at all times, in all things, and in all places, for the rest of their lives. Alma explains that those who do this will be redeemed by God, rise in the first resurrection, and receive eternal life. His main point is that baptism is a lifelong promise to love others and to stand up for God, even when it is hard. The people were so happy to make this covenant that they clapped their hands for joy.

Mosiah 22:7.context: Gideon, the king's trusted captain, is speaking to King Limhi, the son of King Noah, in the land of Nephi. Limhi's people were in bondage to the Lamanites, paying heavy tribute, and after being humbled they had turned to the Lord and covenanted to serve Him. When Ammon arrived from Zarahemla, Limhi and Ammon gathered the people to find a way to escape, but the Lamanites were too many to fight. In this verse Gideon offers a plan: pay the Lamanites their last tribute of wine so the guards get drunk, then slip out through a secret pass while they sleep. The plan worked, and Limhi's people escaped into the wilderness and eventually reached Zarahemla. Mormon included this account to show how the Lord delivered a people who had humbled themselves and turned to Him.

Mosiah 24:15.context: This verse comes from Mormon's account of Alma and his people after they left the Waters of Mormon and built a city called Helam. Lamanites and Amulon, a former wicked priest of King Noah, took control of them and put heavy burdens on their backs, and even forbade them to pray out loud. The people prayed silently in their hearts, and the Lord promised to ease their burdens so they could know He was with them. In this verse the Lord keeps that promise: He did not take the burdens away right then, but He strengthened the people so they could carry them easily. They responded by accepting the Lord's will "cheerfully and with patience." The main point is that trusting the Lord and keeping our covenants does not always remove our trials, but He can give us strength to bear them until He delivers us.

Alma 2:19.context: This verse is part of Mormon's abridged account of a dangerous time about five years after the Nephites began to be ruled by judges instead of kings. A man named Amlici wanted to become king, and when the people voted against him, his followers chose him as their king anyway and went to war against the Nephites. Alma the Younger, who was then the chief judge, led the Nephite armies to meet them near the river Sidon. The battle was hard and many on both sides died, as this verse sadly records, but the Nephites prevailed because the Lord strengthened them when they called on Him. Mormon includes this story to show that the Lord upheld the Nephites when they defended their freedom and their right to worship, and it reminds us how much harm pride and the desire for power can cause.

Alma 5:14.context: Alma the Younger is speaking here after giving up his job as chief judge so he could spend his time preaching and help the people remember their duty to God. He is talking to the members of the Church in the city of Zarahemla, many of whom had grown proud and careless. Alma asks them a series of searching questions, beginning with whether they have truly been spiritually born of God and felt a mighty change in their hearts. He also asks whether they have received God's image in their countenances, meaning whether their faces and lives have begun to reflect the Savior. His main point is that real conversion is more than belonging to the Church; it is a deep change of heart through Jesus Christ that shapes who we are and how we live.

Alma 5:26.context: Alma the Younger is preaching to the Church members in Zarahemla after leaving the judgment seat to call the people back to God. Earlier in his sermon he reminded them how the Lord had changed the hearts of their fathers and asked whether they had felt that same mighty change themselves. In this verse he asks a gentle but important follow-up question: if they once felt a change of heart and wanted to sing the song of redeeming love, can they feel that way now? Singing that song means feeling such joy and gratitude for the Savior's redemption that you want to praise Him. Alma's main point is that conversion is not a one-time event, and each of us should check whether our love for Jesus Christ is still alive today and renew it if it has faded.

Alma 7:11.context: After preaching in Zarahemla, Alma the Younger traveled to the city of Gideon, where the people were trying to live righteously. In this verse he is teaching them about the coming of Jesus Christ, who would be born of Mary and live among His people. Alma explains that the Savior would go through pains, afflictions, and temptations of every kind. He says this would fulfill the prophecy that the Messiah would take upon Himself the pains and sicknesses of His people. Alma's main point is that Jesus Christ did not suffer only for our sins; He also chose to experience our sorrows and struggles, so no one is ever alone in what they go through.

Alma 7:12.context: Alma the Younger is speaking to the faithful people in the city of Gideon, continuing his testimony about what Jesus Christ would do when He came to earth. In the verse before, he said the Savior would suffer pains, afflictions, and temptations of every kind. Here Alma adds that Christ would take upon Himself death so He could break the bands of death for all people through the Resurrection. He also teaches that the Savior would take upon Himself our weaknesses so that He would be filled with mercy and know from His own experience how to help us. The word succor means to help or to run to someone's aid, and Alma's main point is that because Jesus truly understands our pain, He knows exactly how to come to our rescue.

Alma 22:18.context: This is the prayer of Lamoni's father, the king over all the Lamanites, after the missionary Aaron, one of the sons of Mosiah, taught him about the Creation, the Fall, and the plan of redemption through Jesus Christ. Earlier, when his life was in danger, the king had offered to give up half his kingdom to save himself. Now, wanting the joy Aaron described, he offered to give up his whole kingdom, and Aaron told him that if he would repent and pray in faith, he would receive what he hoped for. The king bowed before the Lord and promised to give away all his sins to know God, and he was then overcome by the Spirit and fell as if dead. The main point is that knowing God is worth more than anything we own, and the greatest thing we can give up for Him is our sins.

Alma 26:12.context: Ammon, one of the sons of Mosiah, is speaking to his brothers Aaron, Omner, and Himni after about fourteen years of missionary work among the Lamanites. As he remembers the thousands of Lamanites who had been converted, he is filled with so much joy that Aaron worries he is getting carried away and boasting. Ammon answers that he is not boasting about himself at all. He admits that on his own he is nothing and weak, but he glories in God, because with the Lord's strength he can do all things, and he praises the Lord for the miracles they have seen. His main point is that every good thing that happened came from God's power and mercy, so the glory belongs to Him.

Alma 32:21.context: Alma the Younger is teaching a group of poor Zoramites who had been cast out of their places of worship because of their humble clothing. The wealthy Zoramites had turned away from Christ and worshipped on a high tower called the Rameumptom, but these poor people had been humbled and were ready to listen. Alma points out that many people say they will believe only if they are shown a sign from heaven, so he explains what faith really is. He teaches that faith is not having a perfect knowledge of something; instead, it means hoping for things that are not seen but are true. Alma's main point is that we do not need to know everything before we start believing, because faith can begin with hope in true things we cannot yet see.

Alma 32:28.context: Alma the Younger is teaching the humble, poor Zoramites, who had been cast out by the proud members of their own people and had asked him what they should do. He invites them to try an experiment on his words, even if all they have at first is a desire to believe. In this verse he compares the word of God to a seed planted in the heart. If they do not throw the seed out through unbelief, they will feel it begin to swell and grow, enlarging their souls and enlightening their minds. Alma's main point is that we can test God's word for ourselves, and when we nourish it, we will feel the good results and our faith will grow step by step.

Alma 34:32.context: Amulek, Alma's missionary companion, is speaking to the same group of humble Zoramites right after Alma finished his sermon about planting the word like a seed. Amulek adds his own testimony that Jesus Christ is the Son of God and that His great and last sacrifice makes it possible for everyone to be saved. He then urges the people to pray, to care for the needy, and to repent now. In this verse he teaches that this life is the time to prepare to meet God and to do the work we came here to do. His main point is that we should not put off repenting and following Christ, because the time to change is today.

Alma 36:3.context: Alma the Younger is speaking to his son Helaman near the end of his life, giving him personal counsel before Helaman takes charge of the sacred records. Alma begins by reminding Helaman how God freed their ancestors from captivity, because only the Lord could have delivered them. In this verse he points out that Helaman is still young and pleads with him to listen and learn. Alma then testifies that anyone who trusts in God will be supported in their trials, troubles, and afflictions and will be lifted up at the last day. His main point is that trusting God does not mean we will never have hard times, but it does mean the Lord will help us through them.

Alma 36:18.context: Alma the Younger is telling his son Helaman the story of his own conversion, which happened when he was a young man trying to destroy the Church. An angel appeared to him and the sons of Mosiah, and for three days Alma was tormented by the memory of his sins. In the middle of that pain, he remembered hearing his father teach that Jesus Christ would come to atone for the sins of the world. In this verse Alma describes how he cried out in his heart, asking Jesus, the Son of God, to have mercy on him. His main point is that turning to Jesus Christ is the way out of the darkness and pain of sin, no matter how far someone has gone.

Alma 36:20.context: Alma the Younger is still sharing his conversion story with his son Helaman. He has just explained that when he cried out to Jesus Christ for mercy, he could no longer remember his pains and was no longer tormented by the memory of his sins. In this verse he describes the wonderful joy and marvelous light that filled his soul. He says that his joy was just as great as his suffering had been. Alma's main point is that repentance through Jesus Christ does not just take away pain; it replaces it with joy and light, which is why repentance is something to be glad about rather than afraid of.

Alma 37:6.context: Alma the Younger is talking to his son Helaman as he hands him the plates of brass and the other sacred records of the Nephites. He commands Helaman to keep the records safe and to continue writing the history of the people. Alma knows that someone might think it is foolish to take such care over some engraved metal plates. He explains that by small and simple things, great things are brought to pass, and the Lord often uses small means to accomplish His purposes and to confound the wise. His main point is that God works through things that seem small, like scriptures, prayer, and daily obedience, to bring about great blessings, including bringing many people to know Him.

Alma 37:35.context: Alma the Younger is finishing his counsel to his son Helaman, who is still young and is about to become the keeper of the sacred records and a leader in the Church. Alma has just told Helaman to teach the people to resist temptation through faith in Jesus Christ and to be humble. In this short verse he speaks tenderly, asking his son to remember his words and to learn wisdom while he is young. Specifically, he urges Helaman to learn early in life to keep God's commandments. Alma's main point is that youth is the best time to build the habit of obeying God, because those choices shape the rest of our lives.

Alma 37:37.context: Alma the Younger is continuing his loving counsel to his son Helaman, after urging him to learn wisdom in his youth and to let his thoughts and the affections of his heart be centered on the Lord. In this verse he tells Helaman to counsel with the Lord in everything he does, promising that God will guide him for good. Alma gives practical advice: pray to the Lord when you lie down at night so He can watch over you as you sleep, and wake up in the morning with a heart full of thanks to God. He promises that those who do these things will be lifted up at the last day. His main point is that a close, everyday relationship with God through prayer brings His guidance and protection.

Alma 41:10.context: Alma the Younger is speaking to his son Corianton, who had made serious mistakes while serving as a missionary among the Zoramites. Corianton had questions about what happens after death, and Alma has been explaining the resurrection and the law of restoration, which means that in the end we receive back the kind of life we chose, good for good and evil for evil. Alma warns Corianton not to think that restoration means he could be brought from sin straight to happiness. He states plainly that wickedness never was happiness. His main point is that real happiness only comes from living God's commandments and repenting through Jesus Christ, not from doing wrong.

Alma 42:8.context: Alma the Younger is still teaching his son Corianton, who was troubled by the idea that it seemed unfair for sinners to be punished. Alma explains that after Adam and Eve partook of the forbidden fruit, the Lord placed cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the tree of life so they would not eat from it and live forever with no time to repent. In this verse he says it was not wise for mankind to be saved from physical death at that time, because that would have destroyed the great plan of happiness. Instead, God gave people a time on earth to learn, make choices, and repent. Alma's main point is that mortal life, and even death, are part of Heavenly Father's loving plan, which works through the Atonement of Jesus Christ.

Alma 48:17.context: In this verse Mormon, who abridged the Nephite records, pauses his account of the wars to describe the character of Captain Moroni, the young leader of the Nephite armies. While the wicked Amalickiah was stirring up the Lamanites to attack, Moroni was preparing his people to defend their families, their freedom, and their faith. Mormon explains that Moroni did not love bloodshed, was firm in the faith of Christ, and was thankful to God for his many blessings. He then makes a remarkable statement: if all people were like Moroni, the powers of hell would be shaken forever and the devil would have no power over people's hearts. Mormon's main point is to hold Moroni up as an example of the kind of faithful, steady person we can all become.

Alma 50:14.context: This verse comes from Mormon's abridged account of how Captain Moroni prepared the Nephites after their recent victories over the Lamanites. Rather than relaxing, Moroni had his people dig earthen walls, build strong fences and towers, and drive the Lamanites out of the eastern wilderness. The Nephites then began building new cities in the land they had secured, including a city called Moroni by the east sea. This verse tells how they also started a city between the cities of Moroni and Aaron and named it Nephihah. Mormon includes these details to show that the Nephites kept preparing and strengthening themselves during a time of peace, a reminder that we can strengthen our own lives against temptation before trouble comes.

Alma 56:47.context: This verse is from a letter Helaman wrote to Captain Moroni, reporting on the war in the southwest part of the land. Helaman was leading 2,000 young men whose parents were Lamanite converts known as the people of Ammon, who had promised never to fight again. Because their parents could not take up arms, these sons volunteered to defend the Nephites, and they asked Helaman to be their leader. Helaman writes that even though they had never fought before, they did not fear death and cared more about their fathers' liberty than their own lives. His main point is that their courage came from faith, because their mothers had taught them that if they did not doubt, God would deliver them.

Alma 62:42.context: This verse comes from Mormon's abridged account of the end of a long, hard war between the Nephites and the Lamanites. After years of fighting, Captain Moroni and the Nephite armies finally drove the Lamanites out of their lands. Mormon records that Moroni strengthened the places most open to attack and then returned home to Zarahemla, while Helaman went back to his own home and soon returned to preaching. At last peace was established again among the Nephites. This matters because the war had affected people in different ways, hardening many but humbling many others, and the humble Nephites were now ready to turn to the Lord and rebuild the Church.

Helaman 1:20.context: This verse is part of Mormon's abridged history of the Nephites at the start of the book of Helaman. After the chief judge Pahoran died, his sons argued over who would take his place, and the new chief judge, his son Pahoran, was murdered by a man named Kishkumen, leaving the Nephites divided and their government in confusion. Because of all this contention, the Nephites did not keep enough guards around their great capital city, Zarahemla. A Nephite dissenter named Coriantumr led a huge Lamanite army so quickly that the Nephites had no time to gather. In this verse Coriantumr cuts down the guards at the city's entrance, marches in, and takes over the whole city. Mormon shows how contention and pride weakened the Nephites and left them open to danger, a pattern that repeats throughout the book of Helaman.

Helaman 5:12.context: These are words that Helaman, a righteous prophet and record keeper, had spoken to his sons Nephi and Lehi before he died. Years later, when many Nephites had become wicked and proud, Nephi gave up being chief judge so he and Lehi could spend all their time preaching, and the brothers remembered their father's counsel. Helaman had named his sons after their righteous ancestors so they would remember those good men and follow their example. In this verse he asks them to remember that they must build their lives on the rock of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. He promises that when the devil sends temptations and trials like a fierce storm with wind and hail, those storms will have no power to pull them down. His main point is that Jesus Christ is a sure foundation, and anyone who builds on Him will not fall.

3 Nephi 4:7.context: This verse is part of the history Mormon abridged, describing a time shortly before Jesus Christ came to the Americas. The Gadianton robbers, led by Giddianhi, had threatened to destroy the Nephites, so the chief judge Lachoneus gathered the people together into one place with food, weapons, and strong fortifications, and he called on them to repent and pray. In this verse the robbers finally march out to battle, dressed in a strange and frightening way meant to strike fear into the Nephites. Mormon describes how terrible they looked so that readers can see how great the danger was. In the next verses, the Nephites fall to the ground and cry to the Lord for help, and then they stand and meet their enemies in the strength of the Lord. The main point is that people who prepare and turn to God in faith do not need to be ruled by fear, even when the threat looks overwhelming.

3 Nephi 5:13.context: Here Mormon, the prophet who abridged most of the Book of Mormon, pauses his history to speak directly about himself. He has just told how the Nephites defeated the Gadianton robbers and turned back to the Lord, and he stops to explain who he is and why he is writing. He is speaking to everyone who will one day read his record, including us. In this verse he humbly introduces himself as a disciple of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who has been called to share Christ's word so that people can have everlasting life. A disciple is someone who follows Jesus and is learning to think and act as He does. Mormon wants readers to know that his whole record was written to bring people to the Savior, and that each of us can also choose to be a disciple of Jesus Christ.

3 Nephi 9:20.context: After Jesus Christ died in Jerusalem, terrible storms, earthquakes, and fires struck the Nephite lands, and then thick darkness covered everything for three days. In that darkness, the people who survived heard the voice of Jesus Christ speaking to all of them, telling them what had happened and inviting them to return to Him. For hundreds of years they had offered animal sacrifices under the law of Moses, which pointed forward to the Savior's own sacrifice. Now that He had given His life, the Lord tells them those offerings are finished, and He asks instead for a new kind of sacrifice: a broken heart and a contrite spirit. This means offering Him a humble, repentant heart that is willing to change, and He promises that those who do will receive the Holy Ghost, sometimes so gently that they do not even notice it at first. The main point is that the Savior wants our hearts, and He is eager to forgive and bless everyone who comes to Him.

3 Nephi 11:10.context: Some time after the darkness ended, about 2,500 people gathered at the temple in the land Bountiful, talking about the great changes in the land. They heard the Father's voice from heaven introducing His Beloved Son, and then they saw a man dressed in a white robe come down out of heaven and stand among them. In this verse, the risen Jesus Christ stretches out His hand and speaks His first words to the people. He tells them plainly who He is: the very Jesus Christ whom their prophets had testified would come into the world. For more than 600 years, Book of Mormon prophets had looked forward to this moment, and now it was fulfilled before their eyes. The main point is that Jesus Christ is real, He is the promised Savior, and He keeps His promises to His people.

3 Nephi 12:48.context: The resurrected Jesus Christ is teaching the Nephites gathered at the temple in Bountiful, in a sermon much like the Sermon on the Mount He gave in Galilee. The people had lived the law of Moses, and now the Savior is teaching them a higher law that reaches into their hearts, such as loving their enemies and not staying angry. This verse is the conclusion of that teaching, where He tells them He wants them to be perfect, even as He and their Father in Heaven are perfect. Speaking now as the resurrected Lord, He names Himself alongside the Father as an example of that perfection. Becoming perfect does not mean never making a mistake in this life; it means becoming complete and whole over time, with His help. The main point is that the Savior invites us to keep growing to become like Him and our Heavenly Father, and that perfection ultimately comes as a gift through His grace.

3 Nephi 18:15.context: On His first day with the Nephites at the temple in Bountiful, the risen Jesus Christ had healed their sick, blessed their children, and introduced the sacrament. In this verse He is speaking to His twelve chosen disciples, right after teaching about the sacrament and before turning back to the whole multitude. He warns them that they must watch and pray always so that the devil will not tempt them and lead them away. Watching means staying spiritually alert, and praying always means staying close to Heavenly Father throughout each day. In the verses that follow, Jesus gives the same counsel to all the people and asks them to pray in their families too. The main point is that constant prayer is a protection, giving us the strength we need to resist temptation and stay on the Lord's path.

3 Nephi 27:20.context: Near the end of His ministry among the Nephites, Jesus Christ appeared to His twelve disciples while they were traveling, preaching, and fasting together. They had asked Him what to name His Church, and He answered that it should be called by His name and built on His gospel. Then He explained exactly what His gospel is: He came into the world to do His Father's will and was lifted up on the cross so that all people could be drawn to Him. In this verse He gives the commandment at the heart of that gospel: repent, come unto Him, be baptized in His name, and receive the Holy Ghost. He promises that by doing this, people can be made clean and stand spotless before Him at the last day. The main point is that the gospel of Jesus Christ is simple and is offered to everyone, everywhere, through faith, repentance, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost, and staying faithful to the end.

3 Nephi 27:27.context: In this verse the risen Jesus Christ is speaking to His twelve Nephite disciples, near the end of His time with the Nephites. He has just taught them what His gospel is and told them to keep careful records, because people will be judged by what is written. Here He tells the Twelve that they will help judge their people, using the fair judgment He will give them. Then He asks them an important question about what kind of people they should be, and He answers it Himself: they should be even as He is. This is more than a suggestion; it is what His followers are meant to work toward through their covenants with Him. The main point is that Jesus Christ is our perfect example, and every disciple is invited to become more like Him each day.

4 Nephi 1:15.context: The book of 4 Nephi is Mormon's short summary of almost 300 years of history after Jesus Christ visited the Americas. After the Savior's visit, the people on the whole land were converted, both Nephites and Lamanites, and they shared all things in common. In this verse Mormon explains why there was no contention among them: the love of God lived in their hearts. Because of that love, there were no divisions, no fighting, and no separate groups, and they became one people, the children of Christ. Mormon says there could not have been a happier people among all those God had created. The main point is that when people truly follow Jesus Christ and fill their hearts with God's love, they can live together in peace and unity.

4 Nephi 1:46.context: This verse comes near the end of 4 Nephi, Mormon's summary of the years after the Savior's visit. For about two hundred years the people had lived in peace and unity, but pride slowly crept in, people began dividing into groups again, and some even taught their children to hate. By the time three hundred years had passed, both the Nephites and the Lamanites had become very wicked. In this verse Mormon reports that the Gadianton robbers, a secret band working for power and gain, had spread across the whole land, and the only righteous people left were the disciples of Jesus. The people were storing up great wealth and trading in all kinds of goods, showing their hearts had turned from God to riches. The main point is that even a wonderfully blessed people can lose their happiness when they let pride and love of riches replace the love of God.

Mormon 2:8.context: In this verse Mormon is writing about his own life, during a time of terrible war between the Nephites and the Lamanites. Though he was only a young man, he had been chosen to lead the Nephite armies, and he was trying to gather his people together so they could defend themselves. Here he describes how the land was full of robbers and Lamanite armies, and how violence and destruction were spreading everywhere. Saddest of all, even with so much danger and suffering around them, his people still refused to repent of their wicked choices. A few verses later Mormon explains that their sorrow was only about their troubles, not the kind of sorrow that leads people to come to Jesus and change. The main point is that troubles alone do not change a heart; true repentance comes when we turn to the Savior.

Ether 10:10.context: In the book of Ether, Moroni is abridging the history of the Jaredites, an ancient people who came to the Americas long before Lehi's family. Ether 10 moves quickly through a series of Jaredite kings, some righteous and some wicked, and shows how each one affected the people. Just before this verse, a king named Riplakish had burdened the people with heavy taxes and harsh labor until they rose up against him. Many years later his descendant Morianton gained power through war, and in this verse he wins the people's favor by easing the heavy burdens they had carried, so they anoint him as their king. The next verse adds that he was fair to the people but did not keep himself clean, so he was cut off from the presence of the Lord. Moroni includes these stories to show how much the choices of leaders matter, and that being kind to others is important but does not replace personal righteousness before God.

Ether 12:6.context: While abridging the Jaredite record, Moroni tells how the prophet Ether preached to the people from morning until night, urging them to believe in God, but they would not listen because they could not see the things he prophesied. At this point Moroni stops the story to add his own words about faith, speaking directly to all the future readers of his record. He explains that faith is about things we hope for but cannot see yet. He also counsels readers not to argue just because they cannot see, since a witness, or confirmation, comes after our faith has been tested. In the rest of the chapter Moroni gives many examples of people whose faith came first and whose miracles came afterward. The main point is that we often must act in faith before we receive a spiritual witness, and God blesses those who trust Him.

Ether 12:27.context: In Ether 12, Moroni pauses his abridgment of the Jaredite record to share a personal experience. He told the Lord he was worried that people in the future would mock the Book of Mormon because he and the other writers felt weak and awkward in their writing. In this verse the Lord answers Moroni, and Moroni records the Lord's words for all of us to read. The Lord explains that He gives people weakness so that they will be humble, and that His grace is enough for everyone who humbles themselves before Him. He promises that if people come to Him with humility and faith, He will make their weak things become strong. The main point is that our weaknesses can lead us to rely on Jesus Christ, and through His help and grace they can be turned into strengths.

Moroni 6:4.context: After the Nephite nation was destroyed, Moroni lived alone for many years and kept adding to the record, hoping his words would help people in a future day. In Moroni 6 he explains to his future readers how the Church of Christ worked among his people, beginning with who could be baptized. In this verse he describes what happened after baptism: new members were changed and cleansed by the Holy Ghost, and their names were written down so they would not be forgotten. Church members then helped them stay strong by teaching them the word of God, encouraging them to keep praying, and helping them stay on the right path. Moroni wants us to understand that joining the Church is a beginning, not an ending, and that new members need to be cared for and "nourished" like a young plant. Above all, they were taught to trust fully in Jesus Christ, who starts and finishes the work of faith in us.

Moroni 7:16.context: Moroni 7 is a sermon given by the prophet Mormon, Moroni's father, which Moroni copied into the record before burying the plates. Mormon was speaking in a synagogue to faithful Church members, whom he called the peaceable followers of Christ, at a time when the Nephite society around them was growing more wicked. In this part of his sermon, he teaches them how to tell whether something comes from God or from the devil. He explains that the Spirit of Christ, also called the Light of Christ, is given to every person so they can know good from evil. Anything that invites us to do good and to believe in Jesus Christ comes from God, and we can know that as surely as we can tell daylight from the dark night. Mormon's main point is that Heavenly Father has given everyone an inner light to guide them toward what is right.

Moroni 7:45.context: This verse comes from a sermon by Mormon, Moroni's father, which Moroni later wrote into the record. Mormon was teaching faithful Church members in a synagogue during a time when many Nephites had stopped loving one another. Near the end of his sermon he speaks about faith, hope, and charity, and says that charity is the most important of the three. In this verse he lists what charity looks like in action: it is patient and kind, it is not jealous or proud, it does not get angry easily, and it keeps believing, hoping, and enduring. Mormon wants his listeners to see that charity is not just a feeling but a way of living, and these qualities describe Jesus Christ Himself.

Moroni 7:47.context: Mormon, Moroni's father, spoke these words in a sermon to faithful Church members gathered in their synagogue, and Moroni later copied the sermon into the record. The Nephites around them were losing their love for one another, so Mormon taught his listeners about faith, hope, and charity. Just before this verse, he urged them to hold tightly to charity, because everything else will fail but charity never fails. Here he gives the famous definition: charity is "the pure love of Christ," and it lasts forever. He promises that anyone who has this love at the last day will be blessed. Mormon's main message is that charity is more than doing kind things now and then; it is becoming a person who loves others the way Jesus Christ loves us.

Moroni 7:48.context: This is the closing verse of a sermon by Mormon, Moroni's father, given to faithful Church members in a synagogue and later recorded by Moroni. After teaching that charity is the pure love of Christ, Mormon tells his "beloved brethren" how to receive it. He invites them to pray to Heavenly Father "with all the energy of heart" to be filled with this love, which God gives to all true followers of Jesus Christ. Praying this way means praying with real desire and our whole heart, not just saying a quick or careless prayer. Mormon teaches that this love helps us become children of God and become more like the Savior, so that when He comes we will be like Him. His main point is that charity is a gift from God that we can sincerely ask for, and it helps make us pure as Christ is pure.

Moroni 8:18.context: Moroni 8 is a letter that the prophet Mormon wrote to his son Moroni soon after Moroni was called to the ministry, and Moroni later included it in the record. Mormon had learned that some Church members were arguing about whether little children needed to be baptized, so he asked the Lord and received an answer by revelation. He explains that baptism is for repentance and the forgiveness of sins, but little children cannot sin, so they do not need to be baptized and are "alive in Christ." In this verse Mormon gives one reason he is so sure: God does not play favorites, and He never changes from one age to the next. If God saved some children but not others just because of baptism, He would be unfair and changeable, and Mormon knows that He is neither. Mormon wants Moroni and the Church to trust that God is perfectly fair and loving toward every child.

Moroni 10:3.context: Moroni 10 contains Moroni's final words, written just before he buried the plates, more than 420 years after the sign of Christ's birth. He addresses them to the Lamanites, whom he calls his brethren, and to everyone who would one day read the Book of Mormon. In this verse he begins his famous invitation by asking readers to remember how merciful the Lord has been to people from the time of Adam until the day they receive the book. He also asks them to "ponder it in your hearts," which means to think about it carefully and prayerfully. This echoes Nephi's promise at the very start of the Book of Mormon that the Lord shows tender mercies to those who trust Him. Moroni's point is that remembering and pondering God's goodness softens our hearts and prepares us to receive a testimony.

Moroni 10:4.context: Moroni wrote these words as part of his farewell, shortly before he buried the plates, speaking to the Lamanites and to all future readers of the Book of Mormon. After inviting readers to remember the Lord's mercy and ponder it, he gives what is often called Moroni's promise. He invites them to ask God the Eternal Father, in the name of Christ, whether the book is true. He promises that if they ask with a sincere heart, with "real intent," and with faith in Christ, God will show them the truth by the power of the Holy Ghost. Asking with real intent means being ready to act on the answer, not just asking out of curiosity. Moroni's main point is that anyone can come to know for themselves that the Book of Mormon is true by reading, remembering, pondering, and praying.

Moroni 10:5.context: This verse is part of Moroni's farewell message, written as he prepared to seal up and bury the plates, to the Lamanites and to all who would later read the Book of Mormon. Just before this, he promised that God would show sincere readers that the book is true through the Holy Ghost. In this short verse, he widens that promise to cover much more. He teaches that by the power of the Holy Ghost, we may know the truth of all things. Together, verses 3 to 5 are often called Moroni's promise, a pattern of reading, remembering, pondering, and asking that can help a testimony grow, often little by little. Moroni wants readers to understand that the Holy Ghost is a trustworthy teacher who can help them recognize truth throughout their lives.

Moroni 10:32.context: These are some of the very last words Moroni wrote before burying the plates and saying farewell. He is speaking to the Lamanites, to the house of Israel, and to all future readers of the Book of Mormon. Near the end of his message, he gives a heartfelt invitation: "come unto Christ, and be perfected in him." He explains that if we turn away from all ungodliness and love God with all our might, mind, and strength, then Christ's grace is enough to help us become perfect in Him. Coming unto Christ means more than learning about Him; it means trying to become like Him. Moroni's main point is that we cannot become perfect on our own, but as we do our best, the Savior's grace makes up the difference.

Moroni 10:33.context: Moroni wrote this verse at the very end of the Book of Mormon, as he finished his farewell and prepared to bury the plates. He was speaking to the Lamanites and to everyone who would read the record in the future. Continuing his invitation to come unto Christ, he explains what happens to those who are made perfect in Christ by His grace and do not deny His power. They become "sanctified," meaning made clean and holy, through the shedding of Christ's blood, which is part of Heavenly Father's covenant to forgive our sins. Moroni promises that through this process we can become "holy, without spot." His main point is that being made clean and holy is a gift that comes through Jesus Christ's Atonement, not something we can earn alone.
